title: The sisters' songs, three
tomorrow: a man won't let her pass on the road. what does she hand him?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patacara drew the wick down with a needle: the lamp goes out. Her students thanked her with their practice. Today, a sister looks in the mirror.
screen: `THE LAMP GOES OUT.` → `A SISTER LOOKS IN THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Some photo filters will age your face by decades in a second. People laugh, or go quiet, or swipe it away fast. Ambapali did it without a filter. In the stories she's a courtesan of Vesali, praised for her beauty, who gave her mango grove to the Buddha. In the Therigatha, she's an old nun, looking at her own body, part by part, and singing about what she sees.
screen: `A FILTER THAT AGES YOUR FACE.` → `PRAISED FOR HER BEAUTY.` → `NOW AN OLD NUN, LOOKING.`

segments.voice: Today's question: how do you look honestly at getting old? Ambapali's song goes verse by verse, in plain paraphrase. My hair was black as bees, curled at the tips; now it's like bark fiber. My eyes shone like jewels; now they're dim. My teeth were like fresh buds; now they're broken. My hands were smooth; now they're like roots. And after every verse, the same refrain: so it was, and the word of the one who speaks truth is not otherwise. No complaint. No pretending. She agrees with what she sees. A neighbor tradition looks just as hard. Ecclesiastes, in the Bible read by Jews and Christians, describes old age through the body too: the grinders cease because they are few, and, in the King James words, "those that look out of the windows be darkened." Some readers hear teeth and eyes there, as in her song. That's what they share: aging read off the body, honestly, part by part. And the honest difference: Ecclesiastes opens that chapter with "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth," and ends with the spirit returning to God who gave it. Ambapali's refrain turns to the Buddha's word: everything made changes, so it was. Two old voices, facing the same mirror, each in its own words.
screen: `HAIR LIKE BEES, NOW LIKE BARK.` · `SO IT WAS. NOT OTHERWISE.` · `ECCLESIASTES: THE WINDOWS DARKENED.` · `ONE MIRROR, TWO TURNS.` · then, large: `SO IT WAS.`

segments.voice: Look at your hands for the whole sit. The lines at the knuckles, the nails, a scar, the veins. Don't judge them young or old. Just see them as they are today, and when the bell rings, let them rest.
The sisters' songs, today Ambapali's: an old nun reading her body verse by verse, with one refrain: so it was.
So it was: she sang it to her own mirror, without flinching. Day seventeen hundred.

screen: `DAY 1700 COUNTS.` → `THE SISTERS, REREAD · 3 OF 5.` → `TOMORROW: A MAN BLOCKS HER ROAD. WHAT DOES SHE HAND HIM?`

howItsDone: Ambapali's verses are read in Theravada teaching as a reflection on impermanence and the body; Buddhist practice includes reflecting on aging as something everyone born will meet.

fork.setup: your grandmother sighs at an old photo: 'look what happened to me.' which reply is closest to Ambapali?
options: it changed, the way everything does. you're still here looking at it.
you don't look any different at all, honestly
don't look at old photos, they only make you sad
fork.reveal: Ambapali neither denied the change nor turned away from it. she named it, verse by verse, and said: so it was.

original.note: Pali name; amba is mango. She gave her mango grove to the Buddha, and later sang of her own aging.

trapdoor: what you thought: a beautiful woman's poem about getting old must be sad.
what it means: Ambapali reads her body verse by verse and agrees with every change: so it was, the truth-speaker's word, not otherwise.
what a scholar hears: Thig 13.1, a long poem with a fixed refrain; the gift of her mango grove is in DN 16; Ecclesiastes 12 reads old age off the body too, and turns toward God.
guess: poems of the early nuns, here an old nun reading her body
love songs Ambapali sang when she was young and admired

chat.says: Ava's mom saw my hand drawings and quoted Ecclesiastes about getting old. same as Ambapali, or not?
options: alike and not: both read aging honestly; one turns to the Creator, one to the Buddha's word.
exactly the same. every religion says the same thing about aging in other words.
nothing alike. one is about God and one isn't, so there's no overlap at all.
chat.meaning: Ambapali and Ecclesiastes both read old age off the body, honestly. Ecclesiastes turns to God; Ambapali's refrain turns to the Buddha's word. Shared, and different.

Ambapali.meaning: a courtesan of Vesali who became a nun and sang of aging

Vesali.meaning: a city in ancient India where Ambapali lived

Ecclesiastes.meaning: a book of the Bible, a teacher's reflections on life

courtesan.meaning: a woman paid to entertain wealthy men, in old courts

Therigatha.meaning: poems spoken by the early Buddhist nuns

notes: Thig 13.1 paraphrased: hair black like bees, curled at the tips, now like hemp/bark fiber; eyes bright like jewels, now dim; teeth like plantain buds, now broken; hands smooth, now like roots; each verse ends 'so it was, the word of the truth-speaker is not otherwise'. The poem has more verses (voice, nose, ears, breasts, legs, feet); the script picks four. Confirm images and order.
Ambapali as a courtesan of Vesali who gave her mango grove: DN 16 (the grove) and the commentary; hedged 'in the stories'. Confirm.

Unity thread (wisdom day): shared, aging read off the body (Ecclesiastes 12:3 grinders = teeth, windows = eyes, a traditional reading the script lets the listener hear rather than assert); difference, Ecclesiastes 12:1 and 12:7 turn toward God and the spirit returning to God, Ambapali's refrain to the Buddha's word. KJV quotations: 12:3 'those that look out of the windows be darkened', 12:1 'Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth'; 'the grinders cease because they are few' also quoted from 12:3; 12:7 paraphrased. Confirm the KJV text.
'Teeth and eyes, in both' reads Ecclesiastes' grinders and windows as teeth and eyes; the script hedges it as 'some readers hear'; confirm.
